statement: A square napkin is folded in half and then in half again, making a smaller square with sides of 10 cm. What is the perimeter of the napkin when it is unfolded?

choices.misconception: I found the side of the unfolded napkin, 20 cm, and stopped before working out the perimeter.
I gave the perimeter of the folded square, $4 \times 10 = 40$, not the unfolded napkin.
I unfolded only one fold, getting a 20 cm by 10 cm rectangle with a perimeter of 60 cm.
I doubled the side once for each fold, making it 40 cm and the perimeter $4 \times 40 = 160$, but each fold works in one direction only, so the side doubles just once.

hints: Unfold one fold at a time. What happens to the shape?
Each fold in half halves one direction only. Undo the second fold, then the first, and keep track of both side lengths. Then find the distance all the way round.
Undoing one fold gives a rectangle 20 cm by 10 cm. Undoing the other fold gives a square 20 cm by 20 cm. Its perimeter is 4 sides of 20 cm.

solutions.reliable: The two folds go in different directions, because the result is a square. Unfold one: the 10 cm square becomes a 20 cm by 10 cm rectangle. Unfold the other: it becomes a 20 cm by 20 cm square. The perimeter is $4 \times 20 = 80$ cm. The transferable idea: undo folds one at a time, tracking each direction separately.

whyOnTest: Folding questions test running a process backwards one step at a time, and noticing that a fold changes only one direction.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
